title: AI influencers: What consumer sentiment data tells brands
content:
As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?
If you’re a marketer or business owner who is already fully using AI in your digital marketing strategy, then you’re likely already familiar with the concept. You may even be curious about leveraging AI influencers in your influencer marketing strategy.
But how will your target consumers feel about the use of AI influencers? Will they be receptive, or can AI influencers erode the trust you’ve built with your audience? Can AI influencers really save you money compared to working with human influencers? And are all virtual influencers AI? Keep reading for answers to these questions and more.
AI influencers are virtual personas whose appearance, voice, behaviors, or content are created or assisted by generative AI. An example of an AI influencer is Aitana Lopez , who has over 400,000 followers on Instagram. She’s marketed as a virtual fitness and lifestyle influencer and has promoted brands such as Amazon, Victoria’s Secret, Olaplex, and Razer.
Her work as an influencer has reportedly earned her and The Clueless, the Barcelona-based tech company that created her, over $11,000 per month .
AI influencers fall under the umbrella of “virtual influencers,” but make no mistake — while every AI influencer is a virtual influencer, not all virtual influencers are AI-generated. For example, the virtual influencer, singer, and model Miquela Sousa (formerly known as Lil Miquela) was created in 2016 using artist-driven CGI, and her music is created by a collective of singers, songwriters, and instrumentalists—not generative AI.
Over the last decade, Miquela Sousa has worked with brands like Gucci, Prada, and Calvin Klein. She’s also the first virtual avatar to sign with a model agency, having signed to CAA in 2020 and previously being represented by WME.
Brands are dabbling with using AI influencers and virtual models like Aitana Lopez and Miquela Sousa for three reasons — creative control, reduced costs, and scalable content.
Ruben Cruz , founder of The Clueless, says Aitana Lopez was created so the company could make a “better living and not be dependent on other people who have egos” or “who just want to make a lot of money by posing.”
In other words, Cruz wanted to avoid working with influencers whose personalities, creative processes, and work styles clash with his company’s creative vision—a sentiment brands wanting to leverage AI influencers can relate to.
AI and virtual creators will recite a script, deliver a video, or conform to a brand’s aesthetic exactly as agreed upon. Companies never have to worry about unwanted input or script changes that could slow production.
The initial creation of an AI influencer or virtual internet personality can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few hundred thousand. However, once out of the initial setup phase, AI influencers can save companies money on lighting, production, and paid partnerships.
Human influencers need to sleep, eat, take breaks, pick up their kids from school, or walk the dog — they can’t make content 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. But AI influencers can. Though AI influencers like Aitana Lopez may look super busy doing their makeup, traveling, and hopping into luxury cars, it’s all fake— so they always have time to make content.
Many consumers feel that AI influencers corrode trust, with one Reddit user saying, “If I see something that is AI but tries to appear real, it’s an instant turn-off and trust killer. It’s enough for me to see it once for a brand, and the trust is gone forever.”
The skepticism toward AI influencers shows up in surveys, too. According to a study published via ResearchGate , 45.3% of consumers would view an ad with an AI influencer without taking action, 28.3% would ignore the ad completely, and only 26.4% would actively engage with the ad, such as by clicking or searching.
AI influencers pose a high risk of eroding trust between brands and consumers because using a fake person to promote a brand’s goods or services doesn’t read as authentic. The appeal of human influencers and content creators is that they’re real people who cultivated a consistent following by being their genuine selves.
Influencers and content creators bond with their followers over shared interests, hobbies, and beliefs, and they often get their audience interested in a product or service by using it themselves.
In fact, a survey by Clutch shows that if a human influencer is found to use AI-generated content, 71% of consumers say they would question the recommendation, and 53% are less likely to buy from a brand known for using AI in social content.
An AI or virtual influencer can’t use a product or service, can’t have a genuine interest, nor a human experience to connect with human followers.
That said, the trust risk is not equal in every situation. It concentrates where audiences are skeptical, where safeguards are missing, where disclosure is weak, and where nobody is measuring the effect. Score each area below before you decide to leverage AI influencers.
Why these four areas matter: Consumers aren’t rejecting AI across the board. That same Clutch survey also found that 42% view AI positively when it’s used for educational content, but 64% would trust a brand or creator less if AI were used to misrepresent products. Nearly 90% say it’s important to disclose AI-generated content.
Disclosure is also becoming a legal matter. For example, as of June 9, 2026, New York requires certain ads featuring AI-generated human performers to include a disclosure, and the EU’s Article 50 transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026. Always double-check to confirm what applies to your markets.
Virtual influencers have been working with brands for years, so their campaigns show what works and what doesn’t. Each example below is broken down by what it teaches about creativity, community, transparency, representation, and governance.
PacSun teamed up with Miquela for its back-to-school and holiday 2022 campaigns, and said the deal marked the start of a broader push into virtual influencers. The two collaborated on social content to amplify those seasonal campaigns after both had taken part in the ComplexLand digital event.
The partnership was built around a persona who already lived online , with roughly 3 million Instagram followers at the time. Choosing a virtual star with an existing audience meant the brand didn’t have to build one from scratch.
The fit rested on shared audience territory. PacSun framed the move as a way to strengthen its connection with a core demographic exploring the digital space. Takeaway: pick a persona whose community already overlaps with yours.
Miquela is open about being a virtual influencer, describing herself as a “Robot living in LA,” so there was no deception to manage. The audience was in on it from the start.
PacSun’s president pointed to Miquela’s involvement in the Black Lives Matter movement and the Rally the Vote campaign as aligned with the brand’s values. That raises a fair question for any brand: a persona’s advocacy is authored by its creators, so scrutinize whose voice is really speaking.
A virtual star never ages, clothes always fit perfectly, and she does what you ask, but that control is also a responsibility. Set clear approval processes for any social or political messaging attached to a persona, since you are effectively the speaker.
Sam is Samsung’s own virtual influencer, created in collaboration with Cheil and the Brazilian design firm Lightfarm. She is used mainly in Latin America, and in July 2023, she connected to the regional launch events from Seoul, where she covered the global Galaxy Unpacked event.
In January 2024, she was named Samsung’s AI ambassador ahead of Galaxy Unpacked 2024, where she was set to present products and interview five live influencers from Latin America.
Sam works because she’s integrated into real brand moments rather than confined to social posts. She has blogged, made tutorials, released a music video promoting the Galaxy Z Flip 5, and helped sell devices at Unpacked events.
Giving a persona several jobs, from host to educator to performer, builds her into the brand’s story rather than treating her as a one-off stunt.
Samsung paired Sam with real people. At Unpacked 2024, she interviewed Latin American creators live, bridging the virtual and human sides of the community. Her role was also regionally focused, which suggests a persona can work better as a local community figure than as a global one.
Sam is openly presented as a virtual influencer, and Samsung’s own newsroom calls her one. Her role is also clear (host, guide, ambassador), so audiences aren’t asked to believe she personally uses Samsung products.
As a brand-owned character, Sam’s look, voice, and personality are entirely Samsung’s choices. Treat that as a casting decision: involve regional teams and creators in shaping a persona who will speak to their audience, rather than designing her centrally and exporting her.
Samsung reported that Sam helped boost early sales of its new devices in Latin America, including a 30% increase in sales on its Mexico live-shopping portal.
Set measurable goals and a content plan before launch, attribute any performance claims to their sources, and decide in advance who will maintain the persona, since a neglected virtual influencer can quickly feel stale.
Kyra was launched by FUTR Studios in January 2022 as a virtual influencer that is both CGI and AI-powered. Her first brand partner was boAt for the #FutureOfAudio campaign, which launched its Rockerz 330 and 333 ANC neckbands.
Amazon Prime Video followed, integrating Kyra into the promotion for its sci-fi series “The Peripheral,” with her creator noting that the team recreated the show’s VR headset and transported her to its setting.
Both campaigns leaned into science fiction, which is where a virtual persona excels. boAt said the collaboration enabled a sci-fi-like audio-visual experience that wouldn’t be possible with any other influencer. Choose briefs a human can’t easily deliver.
The boAt launch reached beyond social posts. Kyra appeared at an in-person boAt party through a 3D projection installation, alongside human creators. Bridging virtual and live moments helps a persona feel part of a scene rather than an ad.
The pairing with Prime Video worked partly because it was an obvious fiction-meets-fiction match. When the story is openly synthetic, disclosure becomes part of the creative rather than a caveat.
Kyra was positioned as India’s first virtual influencer, and her creators said they planned a new model with a South Indian focus . That’s a useful prompt for brands: local relevance matters, and a single persona rarely represents an entire market.
Early results were strong , but they come from launch-novelty periods. Judge a persona on sustained performance, not a debut.
In 2018, Dior’s beauty team had Noonoouri recreate its Rouge Dior Ultra Rouge launch film . The original starred Natalie Portman; the tribute was nearly a shot-for-shot reenactment, down to the Dior ring. Noonoouri also took over the Maison’s Instagram during the Dior Cruise show.
Rebuilding a famous campaign with a stylized animated character created instant buzz. The contrast between the original and the tribute did most of the work.
Dior used the persona to reach younger Instagram audiences interested in high-end beauty. The takeaway is to match a persona to an audience you’re trying to grow, not just one you already have.
Noonoouri’s doll-like proportions make her unmistakably an animation, so nobody is misled about what they’re seeing. A clearly stylized persona carries less deception risk than a photorealistic one.
Her exaggerated features reflect a stylized ideal, not a real body. Brands should consider what beauty standard a digital character promotes, especially in cosmetics.
Stepping into a role originally played by a real actress raises questions about likeness, permission, and optics. Clear agreements around any reference to a real person’s work are essential.
AI can save brands money, but it depends on what you count. AI influencers can cut the most visible line item, production, while adding costs elsewhere: oversight, disclosure, rework, reputation, and measurement. A fair comparison looks at the total cost of the program, rather than the cost of a single post.
You can look up costs online but be aware that cost claims are mostly published by vendors and agencies that sell AI content, and they vary widely. Some guides puts AI influencer creation at $15,000 to $100,000+ upfront , with monthly costs of $500 to $15,000+. But other sources claim 80-95% savings on large volumes of video. Treat all of these numbers as starting points for your own testing, not benchmarks.
1. Production. This is where savings are most credible. Once a persona exists, the marginal cost of producing one more piece of content approaches zero, and there are no talent fees, travel, or scheduling.
The catch is the upfront build and the ongoing work of generating, editing, and approving content. A persona that looks effortless usually still has a team behind it .
2. Risk management. Brands often cite reduced risk of scandal as a draw. In a World Federation of Advertisers finding reported by Favikon, 58% of brands interested in AI influencers named reduced risk of influencer scandals as a top draw. But the risk doesn’t disappear completely; it only changes shape.
You swap the risk of a creator’s behavior for the risk of your own content errors, off-brand outputs, or a backlash against the concept itself. Budget for review and an escalation plan.
3. Disclosure compliance. This cost is growing. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have their own AI labeling rules and protocols. And other countries and regions have legal requirements regarding AI disclosure. In the EU, for example, transparency obligations for AI-generated content began to apply in August 2026.
The direct cost is modest , covering labels, templates, and legal review. The hidden cost is audience trust: consumer distrust is a recognized downside when disclosure is unclear.
4. Rework. Generated content needs corrections: anatomical glitches, inconsistent facial expressions, misreading cultural cues, tone issues. Rework hours rarely appear in a vendor’s cost comparison, so track them in your own use case.
5. PR and reputation. As I said earlier, public perception of AI influencers or synthetic personas ranges from curiosity to hostility, and it varies by category and audience. Set aside time and budget for a communications plan, including how you’ll respond if people accuse you of replacing real creators.
6. Community impact. Human creators bring a ready audience and a relationship with it. A new AI persona has to build both. The savings can also be offset on the other side: some AI adopters found that when creators use AI to cut their own costs, those savings haven’t led to lower fees , because brands pay for influence and credibility.
And partnerships with AI accounts aren’t a sure thing; Data shows that brand deals with AI social accounts fell by about 30% in the first eight months of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.
7. Measurement. Fairly comparing AI and human influencers takes planning. You need matched campaigns, consistent metrics, and enough time to see past the novelty effect. Some of this has a real cost in analyst hours and tooling, and without it, you’re making decisions based on anecdotes.
As one analysis puts it, the honest comparison isn’t a cost debate but a question of what a campaign asks the influencer to do.
They tend to help when you need high volumes of content, many variations to test, a tightly controlled brand look, or multilingual output. They tend to be a poor fit when the sale depends on lived experience or personal credibility, such as skincare results, health claims, parenting, or financial advice.
There, the cheaper post can cost you in conversion and trust.
Before you build a spreadsheet, answer these in plain language. If your team can’t answer them, then you’ll already know you need to reevaluate your strategy.
Then add two summary questions: What is the strongest reason this would save us money, and what is the strongest reason it wouldn’t? Count the “High” ratings. A cluster of them in risk, disclosure, or community impact is a signal to slow down, no matter how good the production savings look.
Once you’ve done the worksheet, a simple model has four parts: one-time setup costs, recurring monthly costs, the hidden costs from your worksheet (rework hours, legal review, monitoring, crisis reserve), and the performance side (conversions, engagement, or sales per dollar spent). Run it against a human-creator pilot of similar scope, and revisit it after a quarter, not a week.
AI influencers can lower the cost of making content. Whether they lower the cost of the program depends on your category, your audience, your compliance exposure, and how honestly you count what’s outside the production line. The brands most likely to come out ahead are the ones that measure the whole picture and start small.
Audiences forgive AI-assisted content that’s honest and consistent. They don’t forgive content that feels off-brand, evasive, or unreviewed. Build the workflow around human judgment, and aim for consistency over perfection.
Write the voice down in a form both people and AI tools can use.
Not every asset needs the same scrutiny. Tier them by risk:
Create templates in advance so disclosure is never improvised. Cover three cases: AI-generated persona, AI-assisted content from a human creator, and paid partnerships. Each should state who made it and whether it’s an ad, in plain language. Have legal review the templates once, then reuse them.
Check requirements for each platform and market, since they differ and are changing.
A content management system, such as HubSpot Content Hub, can serve as a shared home for assets and approval steps, but the process matters more than the tool.
Escalate questions on tone to brand, questions on claims or rights to legal, and questions on audience reaction to social. One person should own the overall workflow so nothing falls between teams.
Hyper-realistic output isn’t the goal. A persona that stays recognizable, sounds like your brand, and is clearly labeled will earn more trust than one that’s flawlessly lifelike but inconsistent. When in doubt, a human decides.
Most backlash comes from a few repeatable mistakes, but each one is avoidable.
The problem: Audiences feel tricked when they discover a persona is AI after the fact, and regulators and platforms increasingly expect clear labeling.
How to avoid it: Say it upfront. Put the AI label in the bio and on sponsored posts, and use plain language rather than burying it in hashtags.
The problem: Almost-human faces, odd hands, and inconsistent features break trust fast and invite mockery.
How to avoid it: Choose a stylization you can execute well and keep it consistent. A clearly stylized character often lands better than a flawed attempt at photorealism. Have a human review every image before it goes live.
The problem: A persona that comments on social issues or endorses products it can’t plausibly use will seem opportunistic, because a company is writing every word.
How to avoid it: Define what the persona will and won’t talk about. Skip causes you aren’t prepared to support with real action, and avoid testimonials that depend on personal experience.
The problem: Using AI to depict diverse identities without involving those communities can read as tokenism, and generative models can reproduce stereotypes.
How to avoid it: Involve people from the communities being portrayed in development and review. Use AI personas alongside human creators rather than as a replacement for them.
The problem: Fully automated posting and replies produce tone-deaf responses, repeated phrasing, and errors nobody catches in time.
How to avoid it: Keep a human in the approval loop for anything public, especially replies, sensitive topics, and sponsored content. Automate drafting and scheduling, not judgment.
The problem: If it’s unclear who owns the persona, the underlying model outputs, or any real person’s likeness or voice involved, disputes can surface at the worst moment.
How to avoid it: Document ownership and usage rights in contracts from the start, including agency and vendor agreements. Record which tools and training materials were used.
I can absolutely see both virtual and AI influencers becoming more common as businesses further integrate AI into their digital marketing strategy, but three shifts are worth planning around: more interactivity, more personalization, and tighter regulation. The regulatory evidence is much stronger than the evidence on the other two, so plan accordingly.
Interactivity: expect more, with thin evidence so far. Industry commentary points to AI influencers paired with chatbots to offer 24/7 personalized engagement. Marketers also describe tracking conversation depth and return engagement as AI-driven interactions grow. Most of this is vendor and agency commentary rather than measured results, so treat it as direction, rather than proof. One practical point is firm, though: if a persona chats with people, EU rules now require that they be told they’re interacting with AI (see below).
Personalization: promised, not yet proven. Brands can use AI personas to give customers more personalized attention without expanding costly support teams. I found no independent data showing this works better than human-led engagement, so test it before building a strategy on it.
Regulation: the clearest shift. Governments are starting to set rules for AI-generated content in advertising, particularly around disclosure. For example, the EU’s AI Act includes transparency requirements for AI-generated content and for AI systems that interact with people.
In the US, New York has passed a law requiring disclosure of AI-generated “synthetic performers” in ads , and the FTC has indicated that its endorsement guidance applies to virtual endorsers as well as human ones. Other jurisdictions are considering similar measures.
Now, I’m not a lawyer and this isn’t legal advice, but I can tell you these rules differ by region and platform, and they change frequently. So, before running a campaign with an AI persona, check the current requirements for each market you’re targeting with qualified counsel.
Rules, platforms, and tools are changing quickly enough that annual reviews will lag. Each quarter, review four things:
Assign one owner to run the review, with brand, legal, and social each contributing.
The timeframes below are suggestions, so adjust them to your campaign cycle.
Phase 1: Limit channels (weeks 1-4). Launch on one or two channels and in a limited set of markets. Start with the markets where disclosure rules are clearest. Write starter creative guardrails before the first post, covering topics to avoid, tone, and approval steps.
Phase 2: Test messages (weeks 4-8). Run small A/B tests comparing AI-persona content with a human-creator benchmark on the same message. Change one variable at a time and measure conversion, not only engagement.
Phase 3: Monitor sentiment (ongoing from launch). Review comments, mentions, and shares weekly. Track whether audience reaction is curious, neutral, or hostile, and flag any confusion about whether the persona is AI. Set a threshold in advance for when you pause.
Phase 4: Codify guardrails and decide (weeks 8-12). Turn what you learned into written rules for visuals, voice, topics, disclosure, and escalation. Then make an explicit scale, hold, or stop decision based on results and sentiment, not momentum.
Expand only after a pilot passes your own criteria. Keeping it small is what lets you change course cheaply.
In practice, yes, and the rules are tightening. Platforms like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube have their own AI labeling requirements. On the legal side, the EU’s AI Act transparency obligations (Article 50) began to apply from 2 August 2026, and they cover content generated or modified with AI.
In the US, the FTC still expects a clear “this is paid” disclosure on sponsored posts. Some sources also report that the FTC treats presenting an AI-generated persona as a real human without disclosure as potentially deceptive, and that several states are moving toward requiring a synthetic-performer disclosure.
Treat the legal details as a moving target and have counsel review any paid campaign, especially if it reaches EU audiences. Beyond compliance, disclosure is also good brand hygiene: audiences tend to react worse to a reveal than to an upfront label.
Use the same core metrics you’d apply to any creator: reach, engagement rate, click-through, conversions, and cost per acquisition. Then add a few that are specific to synthetic personas.
Track audience sentiment (are comments curious, indifferent, or hostile?), brand-lift or recall in the persona’s target segment, and content production efficiency, since one of the main advantages is speed and cost.
Be cautious with headline numbers. Some analyses suggest AI personas can be cheaper than human creators. In contrast, others find human influencers drive higher engagement, so run your own test against a human-creator benchmark rather than trusting industry averages.
Avoid them wherever personal credibility is the product. That includes skincare or supplement claims that rely on real results, health and wellness advice, parenting, financial guidance, and any category where followers expect lived experience.
An AI persona can’t truthfully say “I tried this and it worked for me.” They tend to fit better into visual, aspirational, or entertainment-led categories such as fashion, gaming, and lifestyle.
Also steer clear if your audience is hostile to synthetic content, if you can’t commit to clear disclosure, or if your team lacks the capacity to manage the persona consistently over time. Public backlash against AI-generated models in fashion advertising shows the reputational risk is real.
They can broaden the range of faces and identities a brand shows, but they come with real trade-offs. A brand can create personas across ages, body types, ethnicities, and abilities without a casting budget.
The risk is that this substitutes for hiring and paying real people from those communities, and it can read as tokenism or “representation without the representatives.” Generative models also carry biases from their training data, so outputs often skew toward narrow beauty standards unless you actively guide them.
A sensible approach is to use AI personas alongside human creators rather than instead of them, involve people from the communities being depicted in the creative process, and review outputs for stereotypes before publishing.
Start with a documented voice guide: tone, vocabulary, words to avoid, and example posts that are on-brand and off-brand.
Feed that guide into your prompts or tooling as a standing reference, and keep a fixed character sheet for the persona (backstory, values, visual style) so the look and personality don’t drift between posts. Keep a human editor in the approval loop, especially for anything customer-facing or sponsored.
Finally, audit regularly by comparing a sample of recent posts against your guide, since drift tends to creep in gradually.
